missions.title: Help a spacecraft inspect itself
missions.summary: A robot must observe equipment, locate what it sees, and report useful evidence without requiring constant human attention.
missions.constraint: A measurement is only useful when its location, uncertainty, and meaning are known. The robot also needs a safe response when perception or motion fails.
missions.today: NASA’s Astrobee robots provide an established ISS research platform for free-flying robotics. An enclosed station environment differs substantially from free space.
missions.research: Autonomous inspection and coordinated robot work remain task- and environment-dependent.
missions.horizon: Self-maintaining settlements would require far more capable sensing, repair, logistics, and fault recovery.

missions.title: Build something too large to launch whole
missions.summary: An orbital assembly team has to align parts, make a connection, inspect it, and recover when it does not fit.
missions.constraint: An arm pushes back on its host. Flexible structures change their behavior as they grow. A joint must be inspectable, not merely visually aligned.
missions.today: NASA ARMADAS demonstrates modular robotic assembly research on the ground. It is a useful case in coordinated construction.
missions.research: Taking such capabilities into mission environments requires additional integration, environmental qualification, and validation.
missions.horizon: An orbital shipyard manufacturing arbitrary vehicles from local resources is a much larger leap.

missions.title: Keep somewhere to live working
missions.summary: A habitat must continuously support its occupants, remove waste heat, provide usable resources, and remain maintainable.
missions.constraint: Closing a water loop does not close every material loop. Reliability depends on consumables, repair, power, interfaces, and people.
missions.today: Crewed stations demonstrate long-duration life-support operations with resupply and maintenance. This is not complete independence from Earth.
missions.research: Longer missions require better resource recovery, monitoring, logistics, and maintainability.
missions.horizon: Large self-sufficient settlements remain a conditional possibility, not a scheduled engineering deliverable.

missions.title: Find a path through space
missions.summary: A mission needs to know where it is, where it is going, and which corrections are physically possible.
missions.constraint: Position, velocity, orientation, and time are distinct quantities. Measurements are imperfect; propellant and power are limited.
missions.today: Orbital motion and spacecraft navigation have extensive flight heritage. Our circular model isolates one relationship.
missions.research: Autonomous navigation and mission-specific guidance add constraints well beyond this introductory model.
missions.horizon: Routine travel between large off-world communities depends on infrastructure and economics as well as trajectories.

missions.title: Power the mission. Lose the heat.
missions.summary: Useful computation, sensing, communication, and actuation all need energy and produce thermal consequences.
missions.constraint: Enough stored energy does not ensure acceptable temperatures. Vacuum changes how heat can leave an external surface.
missions.today: Conservation of energy provides the starting point for thermal and electrical accounting. Practical hardware requires detailed analysis and testing.
missions.research: Power availability, operating cycles, environmental conditions, and reliability must be analyzed together.
missions.horizon: Large orbital computing facilities are an engineering and economic proposition, not established inevitability.

missions.title: Make flight understandable
missions.summary: Aircraft design connects the forces on a body to its structure, propulsion, stability, and mission.
missions.constraint: A useful calculation needs an operating condition. A coefficient or a favorable test result is not valid across every speed and angle.
missions.today: Aircraft flight rests on established physical principles and extensive experimental methods.
missions.research: New configurations still need validated analysis, ground tests, flight tests, and operational evidence.
missions.horizon: Future aircraft architectures depend on multiple constraints; a striking rendering does not settle them.

disciplines.name: Space robotics
disciplines.preparation: Geometry, programming, mechanics, and careful measurement.
disciplines.practice: Separate sensing, planning, actuation, and verification in one task.

disciplines.name: Control & estimation
disciplines.work: Infer the state and influence how a machine changes.
disciplines.preparation: Calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, and probability.
disciplines.practice: Compare a predicted response with the measured or simulated one.

disciplines.name: Avionics & embedded systems
disciplines.work: Make electronic systems work within timing and power limits.
disciplines.preparation: Circuits, programming, signals, sensing, and test methods.
disciplines.practice: List the sensors, computations, and outputs of an ordinary device.

disciplines.name: Orbital mechanics
disciplines.work: Connect gravity, motion, and mission geometry.
disciplines.preparation: Vectors, calculus, dynamics, and differential equations.
disciplines.practice: Distinguish altitude from orbital radius in a drawing.

disciplines.name: Structures & manufacturing
disciplines.work: Carry loads with materials and parts that can be made and inspected.
disciplines.preparation: Statics, dynamics, materials, geometry, and structural analysis.
disciplines.practice: Trace a load path through a small cardboard structure.

disciplines.name: Thermal systems
disciplines.work: Account for energy and keep hardware within operating limits.
disciplines.preparation: Thermodynamics, heat transfer, fluids, and numerical methods.
disciplines.practice: Draw a boundary and all its energy flows.

disciplines.name: Fluids & aerodynamics
disciplines.work: Predict forces and behavior in moving fluids.
disciplines.preparation: Calculus, mechanics, thermodynamics, and numerical methods.
disciplines.practice: Make repeated paper-aircraft trials with one controlled change.

disciplines.name: Propulsion
disciplines.work: Match momentum exchange and energy supply to a mission.
disciplines.preparation: Thermodynamics, fluids, chemistry, mechanics, and power systems.
disciplines.practice: Compare the requirements of launch and slow orbit adjustment.

disciplines.name: Space systems integration
disciplines.work: Make interacting subsystems satisfy a mission together.
disciplines.preparation: Engineering breadth, requirements, verification, and communication.
disciplines.practice: Write one requirement that can actually be checked.

disciplines.name: Human habitation
disciplines.work: Keep people supported by maintainable physical and social systems.
disciplines.preparation: Thermal systems, biology, fluids, reliability, and human factors.
disciplines.practice: Map dependencies among air, water, power, heat, repair, and crew.

groups.name: 01 / Begin where you are
groups.summary: Arithmetic, fractions, units, and pictures before symbols.

groups.name: 03 / Understand aerospace systems
groups.summary: Energy, flow, flight, structures, and propulsion.

groups.name: 04 / Connect, compute, communicate
groups.summary: Later previews and habits that bring disciplines together.

textbookGroups.name: Thermodynamics
textbookGroups.preparation: Algebra, units, energy and calculus-based physics. Begin by drawing a system boundary and accounting for energy crossing it.

refs.title: Fundamentals of Engineering Thermodynamics
refs.author: Michael J. Moran, Howard N. Shapiro, Daisie D. Boettner, Margaret B. Bailey
refs.note: Publisher-verified reference for systems, energy, properties and cycles. This is an editorial subject recommendation; no current UCSD assignment is asserted.

textbookGroups.name: Fluids and aerodynamics
textbookGroups.preparation: Vectors, calculus, mechanics and conservation laws before aerodynamic analysis. Try the fluids bridge before opening an advanced chapter.

refs.title: Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics
refs.author: Philip M. Gerhart, Andrew L. Gerhart, John I. Hochstein
refs.note: The UCSD Flow Physics teaching page lists this edition for MAE 101A. This supports that listing only, not a promise about your future section.

refs.title: Fundamentals of Aerodynamics
refs.author: John D. Anderson
refs.edition: 6th edition in the course listing; publisher now shows 7th
refs.note: The same teaching page lists the 6th edition for MAE 104. The existing catalog record links the publisher. Match an assigned edition to your actual course.

refs.title: Modern Compressible Flow: With Historical Perspective
refs.author: John D. Anderson
refs.note: An editorial next reference after thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, for flows where changing density matters.

textbookGroups.name: Fundamentals of propulsion
textbookGroups.preparation: Thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, momentum balances and calculus. Learn how a component changes the whole vehicle before focusing on a performance number.

refs.title: Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Propulsion
refs.author: Philip Hill, Carl Peterson
refs.note: Pearson identifies the authors and edition. This is a later analytical reference, not an immediate purchase requirement.

textbookGroups.name: Space propulsion
textbookGroups.preparation: Conservation laws, thermodynamics, fluids and orbital mechanics. Electric propulsion also brings electromagnetism, plasma physics and spacecraft power into the picture.

refs.title: Rocket Propulsion Elements
refs.author: George P. Sutton, Oscar Biblarz, James H. Morehart
refs.note: Use the existing catalog record for staged reading notes and the publisher source.

refs.title: Fundamentals of Electric Propulsion: Ion and Hall Thrusters
refs.author: Dan M. Goebel, Ira Katz
refs.edition: JPL Space Science and Technology Series, original volume
refs.note: JPL hosts lawful chapter downloads. This is the original Goebel–Katz volume, not a claim about the newest edition. Read after the mathematical and physical prerequisites.

textbookGroups.name: Computational fluid mechanics
textbookGroups.preparation: Programming, linear algebra, differential equations, numerical error and fluid mechanics. A convincing image is not evidence that a simulation is correct.

refs.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics: The Basics with Applications
refs.author: John D. Anderson
refs.note: The UCSD Flow Physics page lists this for MAE 185 and MAE 290C. The course evidence is a dated teaching-page listing, not enrollment advice.

refs.title: An Introduction to Computational Fluid Dynamics: The Finite Volume Method
refs.author: H. K. Versteeg, W. Malalasekera
refs.note: Publisher-verified alternative for finite-volume methods. Compare a model with a known solution and check sensitivity to numerical choices.
